stimuli.text: The temperature of a liquid, in degrees Celsius, is modeled by a differentiable function $$H$$ of time $$t$$, in minutes. Selected values are shown.
The function $$f$$ is defined for all real numbers except $$x = 4$$. Selected values of $$f$$ are shown.
The function $$g$$ is differentiable. Selected values of $$g$$ are shown.
A slope field for a differential equation is shown at the points with integer coordinates.

image.alt: A slope field drawn on the grid from x = -2 to 2 and y = -2 to 2.

stimuli.text: A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity is given by $$v(t) = 4\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{6}\right) - 1$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 6$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at position $$x = 5$$.
Let $$R$$ be the region enclosed by the graphs of $$f(x) = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$g(x) = x^2 - 1$$.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 4x(y + 2)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = 0$$.
Consider the curve given by $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 27$$.
People enter an amusement park at a rate modeled by a differentiable function $$P$$, where $$P(t)$$ is measured in people per minute and $$t$$ is measured in minutes. Selected values are shown.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of $$H$$ over the interval $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$, in degrees Celsius per minute?

options.why: This is the total change in temperature; it still needs to be divided by the elapsed time.
This is the average temperature, not the average rate of change.
This divides time by temperature, which is upside down.

questions.explanation: Average rate of change $$= \frac{H(5) - H(0)}{5 - 0} = \frac{39 - 10}{5} = \frac{29}{5}$$ degrees per minute.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_{1}^{2} \left(-6x^{2} + 4\right)dx$$?

options.why: This subtracts values of the integrand instead of an antiderivative.
Correct. An antiderivative is $$F(x) = -2x^{3} + 4x$$; $$F(2) - F(1) = -10$$.
This is F(b) only; subtract F(a) as well.
This adds F(a) instead of subtracting it.

questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_{1}^{2} f(x)\,dx = F(2) - F(1)$$ with $$F(x) = -2x^{3} + 4x$$. That is $$-8 - (2) = -10$$.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which of the following is the best estimate of $$\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$$?

options.why: Averaging the two sides is never how a limit is found.
This is only the left-hand trend.
This is only the right-hand trend.
Correct. From the left the outputs approach -6; from the right they approach -9. The one-sided limits differ.

questions.explanation: Read the table toward $$x = 4$$ from each side. The left side approaches -6 and the right side approaches -9, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

options.why: This is the derivative of the first factor times the second, without the second term of the product rule.
This differentiates only the exponential factor.
This multiplies the derivatives of the two factors and then drops the exponential.

questions.stem: A quantity $$y$$ satisfies $$\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$$ and doubles every 2 hours. What is the value of $$k$$?

options.why: This is not a solution of e^{kT} = 2.
Correct. $$y = y_0e^{kt}$$ and $$e^{2k} = 2$$.
Solving $$2k = \ln 2$$ requires dividing by $$2$$.
Doubling means e^{kT} = 2; solve with a logarithm.

questions.stem: At what value of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f(x) = -x^{3} - 6x^{2} - x$$ have a point of inflection?

options.why: Inflection points are where f″ changes sign, not where f″ has its constant term.
Sign error when solving f″(x) = 0.
Correct. $$f''(x) = -6x - 12$$ is zero and changes sign at $$x = -2$$.
This is −b/(2a), the vertex formula for a parabola, applied to the cubic's coefficients. Set f″(x) = 0 instead.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = -3x^{2} - 12x - 1$$ and $$f''(x) = -6x - 12$$. $$f''$$ is linear, so it changes sign at its zero, $$x = -2$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{-2x^{2} + 5}{5x^{2} + 9}$$?

options.why: Correct. The degrees match, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients, $$-\frac{2}{5}$$.
This is the ratio of the constant terms, which only matters as x approaches 0.
The outputs grow without bound only when the numerator has the higher degree.
The limit is 0 only when the denominator has the higher degree.

questions.explanation: Divide the numerator and denominator by $$x^2$$: the expression becomes $$\frac{-2 + 5/x^2}{5 + 9/x^2}$$, which approaches $$-\frac{2}{5}$$.

questions.stem: A twice-differentiable function $$f$$ satisfies $$f'(1) = 0$$ and $$f''(1) = 0$$. Which of the following must be true?

options.why: $$-x^4$$ has a maximum, but $$x^4$$ has a minimum with the same conditions.
$$x^4$$ has a minimum, but $$-x^4$$ has a maximum with the same conditions.

options.text: There is not enough information to classify $$x = 1$$.
options.why: Correct. When f″(c) = 0 the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive: $$x^3$$, $$x^4$$ and $$-x^4$$ all have f′(0) = f″(0) = 0.

options.text: $$f$$ has a point of inflection at $$x = 1$$.
options.why: $$x^3$$ has an inflection point there, but $$x^4$$ does not.

questions.explanation: With $$f''(c) = 0$$ the test gives no conclusion. Use the First Derivative Test instead.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} -4x - 5 & x < 4 \\ -4x + 3 & x \geq 4 \end{cases}$$. What is $$\lim_{x \to 4^-} f(x)$$?

options.why: Correct. For $$x < 4$$, $$f(x) = -4x - 5$$, which approaches $$-21$$.
One-sided limits can exist even when the two-sided limit does not.
This value doesn't come from substituting the approach point into the left-hand formula.
This is the right-hand limit (and $$f(4)$$). The left-hand limit uses the formula for $$x < 4$$.

questions.explanation: The left-hand limit uses the piece for $$x < 4$$: $$-4(4) - 5 = -21$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is a solution to the differential equation $$y'' + 25y = 0$$?

options.why: $$y'' = 10$$, which does not cancel $$25y$$.

questions.explanation: Substitute each candidate. For $$y = \sin(5x)$$: $$y' = 5\cos(5x)$$, $$y'' = -25\sin(5x) = -25y$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an equation of the line tangent to the graph of $$f(x) = x^{2} + 3x - 1$$ at $$x = -2$$?

options.why: This slope drops the derivative of $$3x$$.
This swaps the x- and y-coordinates of the point of tangency.
This uses the function value $$-3$$ as the slope.
Correct. The point is $$(-2, -3)$$ and the slope is $$f'(-2) = -1$$.
This applies the power rule to the derivative of the inside instead of to the inside function.
This differentiates the outer power but leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This is the value of the function, not its derivative.

questions.stem: What is $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{2x^2 + 1}\right)$$?

options.why: This leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This differentiates the inside but then substitutes it incorrectly into the outer derivative.
This makes a sign or coefficient error in the outer derivative.
Correct. This is the chain rule: the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at the inside, times the derivative of the inside.

questions.explanation: Treat $$\sqrt{2x^2 + 1}$$ as a composite and apply the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{2x^2 + 1}\right) = \frac{2x}{\sqrt{2x^2 + 1}}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{2} + 3x$$. What value of $$c$$ satisfies the conclusion of the Mean Value Theorem for $$f$$ on the interval $$[-3, -1]$$?

options.why: The MVT guarantees a point strictly inside the interval, and this endpoint doesn't satisfy the equation.
The MVT guarantees a point strictly inside the interval, and this endpoint doesn't satisfy the equation.
This is where f′(c) = 0, the vertex, not where f′(c) equals the average rate of change.
Correct. The average rate of change is $$\frac{f(-1) - f(-3)}{2} = -1$$, and $$f'(c) = 2c + 3 = -1$$ gives $$c = -2$$.
This forgets to square the denominator.
Correct. The quotient rule gives $$f'(x) = \frac{-16}{(4x - 6)^2}$$, and at $$x = -1$$ the denominator is $$100$$.
This divides the derivative of the numerator by the derivative of the denominator, which is not the quotient rule.
This subtracts in the wrong order: the quotient rule is (bottom · top′ − top · bottom′) / bottom².

questions.stem: What is the average value of $$f(x) = -3x^{2} - 3$$ on the interval $$[0, 3]$$?

options.why: This averages the endpoint values, which only works for linear functions.
This is the integral; divide by the length of the interval.
This is the average rate of change of f, not the average value.
Correct. $$\frac{1}{3}\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left(-36\right)$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} kx + 17 & x < 3 \\ x^{2} - 1 & x \geq 3 \end{cases}$$ where $$k$$ is a constant. For what value of $$k$$ is $$f$$ continuous at $$x = 3$$?

options.why: This comes from a sign error when moving the constant term across the equation.
This matches the slopes of the two pieces, which is the condition for differentiability, not continuity.
Correct. Continuity needs $$k(3) + 17 = (3)^2 - 1$$, which gives $$k = -3$$.
This forgets to divide by $$3$$ when solving for $$k$$.

questions.explanation: $$f$$ is continuous at $$3$$ when the left-hand limit equals $$f(3) = 8$$. The left-hand limit is $$3k + 17$$, so $$3k + 17 = 8$$ and $$k = -3$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + 5x - 1$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse function of $$f$$. What is $$g'(-7)$$?

options.why: This takes the reciprocal of a function value, not of the derivative.
This evaluates $$f'$$ at $$-7$$ instead of at the input $$-1$$ with $$f(-1) = -7$$.
This is $$f'(-1)$$; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = x^2$$ and $$y = 4x$$?

options.why: This is the area under the parabola alone.
Correct. $$\int_0^{4} (4x - x^2)\,dx$$: top curve minus bottom curve.
An area is never negative; this subtracts the curves in the wrong order.
This is the area under the line alone.

questions.explanation: The curves meet at $$0$$ and $$4$$. Area $$= \int_0^{4} (4u - u^2)\,du = \frac{4u^2}{2} - \frac{u^3}{3}\Big|_0^{4} = \frac{32}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the curve $$x^2 + y^2 = 169$$ at the point $$(5, 12)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$ gives $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y} = -\frac{5}{12}$$.
This is y/x. The tangent line is perpendicular to the radius, whose slope is y/x, so the tangent slope is −x/y.
This is −y/x, which inverts the correct ratio.
Sign error: moving 2x to the other side makes it negative.

questions.explanation: Differentiate implicitly: $$2x + 2y\,y' = 0$$, so $$y' = -\frac{x}{y}$$. At $$(5, 12)$$ this is $$-\frac{5}{12}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1 + 4x)}{5x}$$?

options.why: This differentiates the numerator and denominator but then inverts the ratio, or applies the rule incorrectly.
$$\frac{0}{0}$$ is indeterminate; it does not mean the limit is 0.
Correct. The limit has the form $$\frac{0}{0}$$, so L'Hospital's Rule applies: $$\frac{4/(1 + 4x)}{5}$$.
This leaves out the chain-rule factor when differentiating the numerator.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately (L'Hospital's Rule): $$\frac{4/(1 + 4x)}{5}$$, which gives $$\frac{4}{5}$$.

questions.stem: A farmer has 160 meters of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river. No fence is needed along the river. What is the largest possible area of the field, in square meters?

options.why: This doesn't account for the two equal sides perpendicular to the river.
Correct. With width $$x$$ perpendicular to the river, $$A = x(160 - 2x)$$, maximized at $$x = 40$$.
This fences all four sides (a square), but the river side needs no fence.
This makes all three fenced sides equal, which is not optimal.

questions.explanation: $$A(x) = x(160 - 2x)$$, $$A'(x) = 160 - 4x = 0$$ at $$x = 40$$, and $$A'' = -4 < 0$$, so this is a maximum. The dimensions are $$40$$ by $$80$$, with area $$3200$$.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = -5$$ and $$\int_0^{6} f(x)\,dx = -3$$, what is $$\int_{3}^{6} \left(3f(x) + 3\right)dx$$?

options.why: The integral of the constant $$3$$ over an interval of length $$3$$ is $$9$$, not $$3$$.
This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$3$$.
Correct. $$\int_{3}^{6} f = -3 - (-5) = 2$$, so the integral is $$3(2) + 3(3)$$.
This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{3}^{6} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{6} f - \int_0^{3} f = 2$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$3 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3 = 15$$.

options.why: The numerator is not the derivative of the denominator, so this is not a logarithm.
Correct. Completing the square: $$x^{2} + 8x + 17 = (x + 4)^2 + 1$$.
Sign error when completing the square.
This divides by the derivative of the denominator, which is not a valid antiderivative.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{1} x\left(x^2 + 1\right)^{3}dx$$?

options.why: Correct. With $$u = x^2 + 1$$, $$du = 2x\,dx$$, the integral is $$\frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{2} u^{3}\,du$$.
After substituting, the limits must change to u-values (from c to 1 + c), not stay 0 to 1.
This forgets the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$ from $$du = 2x\,dx$$.
This evaluates only at the upper limit.
Correct. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with the chain rule, substitute the upper limit and multiply by its derivative.
This evaluates the integrand at both limits; the derivative of an accumulation function only uses the variable limit.
This leaves out the derivative of the upper limit, $$3x^{2}$$.
The integrand must be evaluated at the upper limit, not at x.

questions.stem: A 13-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at a constant rate of 3 feet per second. How fast is the top of the ladder moving, in feet per second, when the bottom is 5 feet from the wall?

options.why: The top slides down, so its rate is negative.
The two ends do not move at the same speed; their rates depend on the position.
Correct. $$x^2 + y^2 = 169$$ gives $$x\frac{dx}{dt} + y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$$. With $$x = 5$$, $$y = 12$$, $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{5(3)}{12}$$.
This swaps the roles of x and y.

questions.explanation: Let $$x$$ be the distance from the wall and $$y$$ the height. $$2x x' + 2y y' = 0$$, so $$y' = -\frac{x x'}{y} = -\frac{5 \cdot 3}{12} = -\frac{5}{4}$$ feet per second (the top is moving down).

questions.stem: Consider the curve $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 48$$, for which $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - 2x}{2y - x}$$. At which points on the curve is the tangent line horizontal?

options.why: These points do not lie on the curve.
These have 2y − x = 0, where the denominator is zero: the tangent lines are vertical.
Correct. Horizontal tangents need $$y - 2x = 0$$. Substituting $$y = 2x$$ gives $$3x^2 = 48$$.
These are the y-intercepts; there the slope is 1/2, not 0.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 3(t - 1)(t - 5)$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. For which values of $$t$$ is the particle speeding up?

options.why: Correct. The particle speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign.
This misses $$1 < t < 3$$, where both $$v$$ and $$a$$ are negative.
On $$0 < t < 1$$ the velocity is positive but the acceleration is negative, so it is slowing down.
This is where the velocity is negative, which only means the particle moves left.

questions.explanation: $$a(t) = 6t - 18$$ changes sign at $$t = 3$$. $$v$$ is negative on $$(1, 5)$$ and positive elsewhere. Both are negative on $$(1, 3)$$ and both positive for $$t > 5$$.

questions.stem: The region enclosed by $$y = 2x$$ and $$y = x^2$$ is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.why: This squares the difference of the radii instead of taking the difference of the squares.
Correct. $$\pi\int_0^{2} \left[(2x)^2 - (x^2)^2\right]dx$$: outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
This is π times the area of the region, not a volume of revolution.
This uses only the outer radius (a disc instead of a washer).

questions.stem: Using the data in the table and the values on either side of $$x = 6$$, what is the best estimate of $$g'(6)$$?

options.why: This forgets to divide by the change in x.
This divides the output by the input, which is not a rate of change.
This is the change in g without dividing by the change in x.

questions.explanation: The slope of the secant line through the neighboring points estimates the derivative: $$g'(6) \approx \frac{-8 - (-4)}{5} = -\frac{4}{5}$$.

questions.stem: $$\int \left(10x^{4} + 3\cdot\frac{1}{x} + 4e^{x}\right)dx =$$

options.why: The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, not a power of x.
After raising the power, divide by the new exponent.
Correct. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power; the antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|; e^x is its own antiderivative.
This differentiates instead of antidifferentiating.

questions.explanation: Term by term: $$\int 10x^{4}dx = 2x^{5}$$, $$\int \frac{3}{x}dx = 3\ln|x|$$, and $$\int 4e^x dx = 4e^x$$. Add the constant of integration.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{2} \ln(1 + x^2)\,dx$$?

options.why: Correct. Use the calculator's numerical integration.
This is a single rectangle using the right endpoint, a rough estimate rather than the integral.
This is the change in the integrand, not the integral.
This integrates over only half of the interval.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, $$\int_{0}^{2} \ln(1 + x^2)\,dx \approx 1.433$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following differential equations could have the slope field shown?

options.why: Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.
Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.
Correct. Check where the segments are horizontal and where the slopes are positive or negative; this equation matches at every point.
Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.

questions.explanation: Compare slopes at specific points. For example, at $$(1, 0)$$ the field's segment has slope $$1$$, and at $$(0, 1)$$ slope $$0$$, which matches $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^2$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 2\cos\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right) - 0.5$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At what time does the particle first change direction?

options.why: This is a later time; the question asks for the first change of direction.
Correct. The velocity first changes sign at $$t \approx 1.624$$, found by solving $$v(t) = 0$$ on the calculator.
This is an acceleration value, not a time when the velocity changes sign.
This is the initial velocity, not a time.

questions.explanation: A particle changes direction where $$v(t)$$ changes sign. Graphing $$v$$ on the calculator, the first sign change is at $$t \approx 1.624$$.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$y = x^2 - 1$$?

options.why: This is the distance between the intersection points, not an area.
This adds the absolute values of the curves instead of subtracting.
This is the area under the top curve only.
Correct. The curves meet at $$x \approx -1.557$$ and $$x \approx 1.557$$; integrate top minus bottom.

questions.explanation: Store the intersection x-values from the calculator, then $$\int_{-1.557}^{1.557} \left(2\cos\frac{x}{2} - (x^2 - 1)\right)dx \approx 6.215$$.

questions.stem: The function $$g$$ is defined by $$g(x) = \frac{\sin(4x)}{e^{5x} - 1}$$ for $$x \neq 0$$. For what value of $$g(0)$$ is $$g$$ continuous at $$x = 0$$?

options.why: Correct. Evaluating $$g$$ at inputs very close to 0 (or using the limits of $$\frac{\sin u}{u}$$ and $$\frac{e^u - 1}{u}$$) gives $$\frac{4}{5}$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is indeterminate, not 0.
The two small quantities do not shrink at the same rate.
This inverts the ratio.

questions.explanation: For continuity, $$g(0)$$ must equal $$\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$$. Near 0, $$\sin(4x) \approx 4x$$ and $$e^{5x} - 1 \approx 5x$$, so the limit is $$\frac{4}{5} \approx 0.800$$. A table of values near 0 confirms it.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = xe^{-x/2} + \frac{\sin x}{4}$$ on the interval $$[0, 9]$$?

options.why: Correct. Graph f on the calculator and find its maximum on the interval, checking the endpoints too.
This evaluates f at the critical point of the first term alone; the sine term shifts the maximum.
This is where the maximum occurs (the x-value), not the maximum value.
This is the value at the right endpoint, which is not the largest.

questions.explanation: On the calculator, the maximum of $$f$$ on $$[0, 9]$$ occurs at $$x \approx 1.766$$, where $$f(x) \approx 0.976$$. The endpoint values are smaller.

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 55 + 8\sin\left(\frac{t}{6}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 9$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

options.why: This is the average rate of change over $$0 \leq t \leq 9$$, not the instantaneous rate.
This is the temperature itself, not its rate of change.
Correct. The calculator's numerical derivative of $$H$$ at $$t = 9$$ gives -0.194; the temperature is decreasing.
This multiplies the rate by the time, which is not a rate.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate of change is $$H'(9) \approx -0.194$$ degrees Fahrenheit per hour, from the calculator's numerical derivative.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = x^{3} - 12x - 5$$ on the closed interval $$[-3, 5]$$?

options.why: This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.
Correct. Compare $$f$$ at the critical points $$x = \pm 2$$ and the endpoints: the largest value is $$60$$.
This is the absolute minimum value.
This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 23 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 145 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 4$$?

options.why: This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.
This is only the sand added; include the initial amount.
Correct. $$145 + \int_0^{4} R(t)\,dt$$.
This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$145 + \int_0^{4} R(t)\,dt \approx 145 + 109.195 = 254.195$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 2\sin(t)\,e^{-t/6} + 0.3$$. What is the total distance the particle travels over $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\int_0^{5} |v(t)|\,dt$$ on the calculator.
This is the displacement; backward motion subtracts from it.
This is the average speed, not the distance.
This is the speed at the final time.

questions.explanation: Total distance $$= \int_0^{5} |v(t)|\,dt \approx 4.820$$. The displacement $$\int_0^{5} v(t)\,dt \approx 3.341$$ is smaller because the particle moves backward part of the time.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x + e^{x/2}$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse of $$f$$. What is the value of $$g'(3)$$?

options.why: Correct. Solve $$f(x) = 3$$ to get $$x \approx 0.852$$, then $$g'(3) = \frac{1}{f'(0.852)}$$.
This is f′ at the matching input; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.
This evaluates $$f'$$ at $$3$$ instead of at the input where $$f(x) = 3$$.

questions.explanation: Use the calculator to solve $$f(x) = 3$$: $$x \approx 0.852$$, so $$g(3) \approx 0.852$$. Then $$g'(3) = \frac{1}{f'(g(3))} \approx \frac{1}{3.941} \approx 0.254$$.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = \sin\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right) - 0.50\cos x$$. How many relative extrema does $$f$$ have on the open interval $$0 < x < 5$$?

options.why: Count the zeros of f′ where it changes sign; graph f′ on the calculator over the whole interval.
Correct. Graphing $$f'$$ shows it changes sign 4 times on the interval.
Count the zeros of f′ where it changes sign; graph f′ on the calculator over the whole interval.
Count the zeros of f′ where it changes sign; graph f′ on the calculator over the whole interval.

questions.explanation: Relative extrema of $$f$$ occur where $$f'$$ changes sign. On the calculator, $$f'$$ has sign changes at $$x \approx 0.830$$, $$x \approx 2.686$$, $$x \approx 3.400$$, $$x \approx 4.379$$, so $$f$$ has 4 relative extrema.

questions.stem: Let $$R$$ be the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}\,e^{-x/4} + 0.2$$, the x-axis, $$x = 0$$, and $$x = 3$$. What is the volume of the solid generated when $$R$$ is revolved about the line $$y = -1$$?

options.why: This revolves about the x-axis.
This adds the squared radii instead of subtracting the inner radius squared.
Correct. Washers with outer radius $$f(x) + 1$$ and inner radius $$1$$.
This leaves out the factor of π.

questions.explanation: $$V = \pi\int_0^{3} \left[(f(x) + 1)^2 - 1^2\right]dx \approx 26.688$$.

parts.prompt: Find the acceleration of the particle at time $$t = 5.5$$. Is the speed of the particle increasing or decreasing at that time? Give a reason.

rubric.criterion: Gives the correct acceleration.
Concludes about the speed by comparing the signs of velocity and acceleration.
rubric.example: $$v(5.5) \approx -4.785$$. Velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, so the speed is decreasing.

parts.prompt: Find the position of the particle at time $$t = 6$$.

rubric.criterion: Uses the initial position plus the integral of velocity.
Gives the correct position.

questions.title: Rate of people entering a park

parts.prompt: Use the data to estimate $$P'(7)$$. Show the computations and indicate units.

rubric.criterion: Uses a difference quotient on the interval containing the time.
Gives correct units.

parts.prompt: Use a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals shown in the table to approximate $$\int_0^{12} P(t)\,dt$$. Explain the meaning of this integral in the context of the problem.

rubric.criterion: Sets up the trapezoidal sum with unequal widths.
Gives the correct value.
Interprets the integral with units.
rubric.example: The total number of people who enter the park during the first 12 minutes.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$c$$, for $$3 < c < 9$$, such that $$P'(c) = 0$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Mean Value Theorem (or Rolle's Theorem) with its conditions.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is differentiable (so continuous), and $$P(3) = P(9) = 32$$. By the Mean Value Theorem there is a $$c$$ with $$P'(c) = \frac{32 - 32}{6} = 0$$.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time $$t$$, for $$0 < t < 3$$, at which $$P(t) = 70$$? Justify your answer.

rubric.criterion: Answers yes, citing the Intermediate Value Theorem and continuity.
rubric.example: Yes. $$P$$ is continuous, and $$70$$ is between $$P(0) = 71$$ and $$P(3) = 32$$, so the IVT guarantees such a $$t$$.
